title: The Archive of Small Sounds
text:
Every archive has its celebrated treasures: the signed treaty, the faded map, the letter written by someone whose name every schoolchild knows. The Harbor Sound Library, housed in two cramped rooms above a bakery, has none of these. What it holds instead is the ordinary noise of a town: the rattle of a ferry gate, a market trader calling out the price of mackerel, the creak of a wooden pier in a winter wind. Its founder, a retired radio engineer named Dolores Quint, began recording in her twenties, mostly out of habit, and never quite stopped.

Quint is quick to admit that the project looked absurd at the outset. "People assumed I was either lonely or slightly mad," she says. "Nobody thinks a sound is worth keeping until it has gone." Her turning point came when the old foghorn, which had warned ships for generations, was replaced by a silent electronic beacon. Within a month, residents who had grumbled about its racket for years were asking, a little sheepishly, whether anyone happened to have a recording. Quint had forty-one.

Since then the library has grown steadily, though it remains modest by any measure. Volunteers now catalog roughly a thousand recordings, each labeled with the date, the place and, crucially, the weather, since a street sounds quite different in fog than in sunshine. Schools borrow the collection for history lessons, and a local theater company once built an entire play around the recorded chatter of a vanished fish market. Even so, Quint resists the suggestion that the archive is merely sentimental. Sounds, she argues, carry information that photographs cannot: how crowded a place felt, how quickly people spoke, what everyone considered too ordinary to mention in a diary.

The difficulty, as she is the first to concede, lies in deciding what to leave out. A town produces far more noise than any team of volunteers could preserve, and every decision to record one thing is, implicitly, a decision to ignore another. Critics have pointed out that the collection leans toward the picturesque, favoring gulls and church bells over traffic and building sites. Quint accepts the charge with good grace and has begun asking residents to nominate the sounds they would least like to lose. The most frequent suggestion so far, she reports with a smile, is the ferry's rusty gate.

questions.prompt: Which best describes the writer's purpose in the passage?
choices: To argue that sound recordings are more valuable than photographs
To criticize the library for recording only pleasant sounds

To explain the technical methods used to record sound

title: Why Rivers Refuse to Run Straight
text:
Rivers, one might suppose, would prefer the shortest route to the sea. They do not. Seen from a hill or an airplane, almost any river crossing a flat plain looks less like a road than like a dropped ribbon, looping and doubling back as though in no hurry to arrive. This is not caprice. It is the predictable result of how moving water treats the ground beneath it.

The process begins with an almost trivial irregularity: a fallen log, a patch of harder clay, a slight dip in the bed. The current is nudged sideways, and from that moment the trouble compounds itself. On the outside of the curve the water runs faster, gnawing at the bank; on the inside it slows and lets go of the sand and silt it has been carrying. The outer bank retreats, the inner bank grows, and the bend sharpens itself, handing a fresh problem to the stretch below, where the next bend begins. Over decades the loops swell until, in a flood, the river may cut through the narrow neck of land between two curves and abandon the old loop altogether, leaving a crescent-shaped lake behind.

None of this is convenient for people who live nearby. A river that wanders also floods unpredictably, gives up its farmland, and refuses to stay where a map once placed it. For much of the last century, engineers answered by straightening channels, shortening the route so that water could be hurried away. The logic was impeccable on paper. A straight channel carries water faster, and faster water means less standing water in the fields.

The difficulty is that speed does not disappear; it moves. Water rushed through a straightened section arrives downstream sooner and in greater force, and towns that were safe for generations may suddenly find themselves in its path. Meanwhile, the river itself seems unconvinced by the engineers' tidy solution. Left to its own devices, a straightened channel usually begins to bend again, as if quietly restoring the pattern it never really abandoned. A straightened river, in other words, is not a tamed one but merely an unhappy one.

This is why a growing number of planners now speak of "making room" for rivers rather than commanding them. They allow a stretch of floodplain to be flooded on purpose, and in some places they have even rebuilt the curves their predecessors removed. The approach asks for patience and a certain humility, qualities not always associated with civil engineering. But it begins from a sound observation: that a river's windings are not a defect in its design. They are the design.

title: The Paradox of the Helpful App
text:
At Hollis Ridge School, the study-planning app arrived with an almost evangelical reputation. Students entered their exam dates, and the program did the rest: it divided the weeks into neat sessions, reminded them when to start, and congratulated them when they finished. Teachers, who had spent years watching students leave studying until the final weekend, were delighted. For a while, it seemed that a long-standing problem had been solved by a few lines of code.

The trouble, as one geography teacher put it, was that the students became wonderfully obedient and strangely helpless. When the app was unavailable during a network outage, a number of tenth-grade students could not decide what to study first. They had not forgotten the content; what they had lost, or perhaps never acquired, was the habit of choosing. Every decision about priorities, such as which topic was weakest or which deserved an extra hour, had been quietly taken from them. The app had not merely assisted their judgment; it had replaced it.

This is not an argument against technology, nor a nostalgic plea for the days of crumpled schedules. The app's schedules were, by any objective standard, better than those most teenagers would have drawn up unaided. That is precisely what makes the situation so awkward. When a tool performs a task more competently than we do, we are tempted to hand it over entirely, forgetting that the clumsy early attempts were how the skill was developed in the first place. A student who plans badly this month may plan well next year; a student who never plans may never learn to.

Some designers have begun to take this seriously. One proposal is that such apps should gradually withdraw their support, offering detailed schedules in the first weeks and then asking users to make their own choices, intervening only to comment on them. Another suggestion, rather less comfortable for developers, is that the program should occasionally refuse to help. Whether schools would tolerate software that deliberately makes a task harder is another matter, since a product that frustrates its customers is rarely a popular one.

Yet the underlying principle deserves more attention than it receives. Good teaching has always involved a kind of managed discomfort: enough guidance to prevent despair, but not so much that the learner has nothing left to do. An app that removes every difficulty may produce excellent results on Friday and leave a student less capable on Monday. Convenience, in education at least, is not always a gift.

title: From the Furnace: A Conversation with a Glassblower
text:
Interviewer: Most people picture glassblowing as a graceful craft. After a morning in your workshop, I would call it a negotiation with a very hot and very stubborn partner.

Ilse Brandt: [laughing] That is the kindest description I have heard. The glass is never really under your control. It sags when you hesitate and cools when you linger, so the whole art lies in working with its timetable rather than your own. Beginners always want to rush, and rushing is the one thing it punishes immediately.

Interviewer: You trained as a chemist before turning to glass. Did that help?

Ilse Brandt: Less than you would expect. It explained why a flask cracks, which is useful in the abstract, but a chemist writes down the temperature, whereas a glassblower feels it on her face. I had to unlearn the habit of wanting a number for everything. Eventually I could judge the glass by its color, a dull orange meaning it was still forgiving, a paler one meaning it was almost too soft to hold its shape.

Interviewer: Is there a piece you remember with particular affection?

Ilse Brandt: A pitcher that went wrong. I had meant it to be perfectly symmetrical, and one side drooped slightly while it cooled. My first instinct was to throw it away. Instead, I kept it on a shelf and watched people pick it up. They loved it, precisely because it leaned. A flawless object invites admiration; a flawed one invites conversation. I have been making slightly imperfect pitchers ever since, though I admit that deliberately creating a mistake is far harder than accidentally making one.

Interviewer: Do you worry that machines will make your work obsolete?

Ilse Brandt: Factories can already produce glass more cheaply and consistently than I ever will, and I have no quarrel with that. A machine is excellent when the goal is a thousand identical objects. My customers are looking for something else: a trace of the person who made the object, and of the afternoon in which it happened. If I ever turned out perfect copies, I would be competing with the factories on their ground, and I would lose.

Interviewer: What do you say to young people who want to learn?

Ilse Brandt: I tell them to expect to be bad for a long time. The furnace is not cruel, but it is honest, and it does not offer much encouragement in the early years. Those who stay are usually the ones who find the failures interesting rather than humiliating. And I tell them to burn a few fingers early, because after that you stop being careless.

title: What Gets Lost, and What Gets Found
text:
A translator's work is best when nobody notices it. Readers of a foreign novel in their own language rarely stop to think that every sentence they admire has passed through the judgment of someone else, someone who had to decide, hundreds of times a page, which of two imperfect options to choose. Ines Varga, who has spent three decades translating fiction, describes the job as "disappointing people in the most considerate way possible."

The popular belief that some words are simply "untranslatable" strikes her as both true and misleading. It is true in that a word often carries a bundle of associations, historical, social and emotional, that no single word in another language can reproduce. It is misleading because it implies that translation is a matter of finding equivalents, as if two languages were identical maps drawn in different colors. In practice, Varga insists, the translator is seldom hunting for a matching word. She is hunting for a matching effect. A joke that depends on a pun cannot survive intact, but an equally funny joke with a different pun might.

This is where the difficulty becomes philosophical. If the translator replaces the pun, is the result still the author's joke? Purists argue that any such substitution betrays the original, and that a faithful version should stay close to the words even at the cost of awkwardness. Varga is not persuaded. A translation that is faithful to every word, she says, is often unfaithful to the book, since the original was surely meant to be read easily by its own audience. "If the author's sentences glide, mine must glide too. Otherwise I have not translated the novel; I have only translated its dictionary."

Her convictions are not held lightly, but neither are they rigid. She admits that she has made decisions that she later regretted, including the removal of a long, rambling sentence that she thought too difficult for readers, and which a reviewer afterward praised, in the original, as the novel's finest moment. "That taught me humility," she says, "although humility is a poor consolation when the book is already in print."

For students hoping to follow the same path, her advice is surprisingly unglamorous. Read widely in your own language, she says, because a translator is judged more by the quality of her native writing than by her command of the foreign one. The paradox of her profession is that the better she does her job, the less visible she becomes, and she has made her peace with that. Disappearing, she suggests, is simply what it looks like when the work is done properly.

title: The Referee's Dilemma
text:
In youth soccer, the referee is the one participant whom nobody has chosen to see. Parents shout at the referee, players blame the referee, and coaches, who ought to know better, have been known to describe a decision as "a disgrace" with a nine-year-old standing beside them. Yet the same adults would be astonished to learn that, in many local leagues, the person blowing the whistle is a fourteen-year-old earning a small fee.

This arrangement is defended on the grounds of necessity. There are never enough qualified adults willing to give up their weekends, so leagues rely on teenagers who have completed a short course and are then thrown into matches with real emotions at stake. The results are, to put it charitably, uneven. Some of these young referees display a composure that would be creditable in people twice their age. Others quit after a single season, having discovered that the job consists largely of being wrong in public.

The usual response to such abuse is to demand better behavior from spectators, and banners reminding parents to "respect the officials" now hang beside many fields. Their effect is debatable. A reminder to be calm tends to be heard most clearly by those who were never in danger of shouting. A more interesting proposal comes from a league in a mid-sized town that has begun appointing an experienced referee to sit quietly at the edge of the field and observe, not the players, but the adults. If a spectator crosses a line, the observer speaks to him privately at the end of the match, without any announcement or punishment.

Whether this will work remains to be seen, and its advocates are careful not to oversell it. What it does acknowledge, however, is something more subtle than a rule about conduct: that the referee's authority is not a fixed quantity, but a kind of credit that the surrounding community either extends or withdraws. A young referee who feels supported will make braver and more consistent decisions, which in turn earns further respect. One who feels abandoned will tend to avoid controversy, and the match, ironically, becomes less fair as a result.

None of this will make a disputed penalty any easier to accept. Disappointment is, after all, part of the game, and no one is likely to cheer for a decision that goes against his own child. But the principle, if not yet the practice, is clear enough. If we want fair matches, we must start by treating the person responsible for fairness as someone worth protecting.

title: The Slow Return of the Wetland
text:
A generation ago, the town of Alderbrook drained the marsh on its eastern edge with the confidence of people who knew precisely what they were doing. The land was soggy, mosquito-ridden and, by the standards of the day, useless. Within a few years it had become a handful of tidy fields and a parking lot for the new gym. Nobody saw any reason to mourn a swamp.

The first complaints arrived with the rain. Without the marsh to soak up the water, the streams that ran through the town began to overflow after every heavy storm, and the lower streets flooded so regularly that shopkeepers kept sandbags beside their doors. The council responded in the manner councils usually do, by building higher walls and deeper drains. These measures worked for a time, then failed more expensively, and eventually even the most cautious officials began to ask whether the original decision had been a mistake.

The scheme that followed was, in the words of one council member, "an exercise in paying to undo our own cleverness." The town bought back the fields, removed a stretch of the drainage channels and allowed the water to return. The reaction was divided. A group of farmers warned that the project would produce nothing but insects and neighbors' complaints, and several residents wondered aloud why a town in difficulty should spend money on a bog. The council, to its credit, did not pretend that the objections were foolish. It simply asked for time.

The results, after six years, can fairly be described as modest but unmistakable. The wetland now absorbs enough rainwater to spare the lower streets in all but the worst storms. Herons have returned, along with several kinds of frog that the older residents had assumed were extinct locally, and a school group counts the birds each spring. The mosquitoes, it should be said, have not disappeared, though most people agree they are no worse than before.

It would be tempting to treat Alderbrook as a parable, but the town's own officials are wary of that. The wetland did not solve every problem, and a fiercer storm may yet test it. What it did accomplish was to expose an assumption that had gone unquestioned for decades: that land is only valuable when it is doing something obviously useful. As the council chairman remarked at the reopening, "Nature does not send invoices, but it does keep accounts."

title: Memory and the Photograph
text:
Standing before a famous painting, most visitors to a museum now do the same thing: they raise a phone, take a picture, and move on. The gesture seems harmless, even sensible. A photograph is a far more reliable record than a visitor's memory, and it can be consulted at leisure. The assumption behind it is that, having captured the object, we no longer need to carry it in our heads.

Some psychologists have questioned that assumption. In some experiments, participants who photographed objects during a guided museum tour tended to remember fewer of the objects, and fewer details about them, than those who simply looked. The researchers' explanation is plausible, if not yet conclusive: once we know that a camera is keeping the record, our minds seem to release the task. We outsource our remembering, and the effort of paying attention goes with it. Intriguingly, in one variation the effect appeared to weaken when people used the camera to zoom in on a single detail, as if the deliberate choice of what to photograph restored some of the attention that casual snapping had removed.

These findings should be handled carefully. Such studies are often small, the settings artificial, and real life is far messier than a laboratory. Later work has not always found the same pattern, and some of it suggests that taking photographs can make an experience more enjoyable. A holiday photograph can bring back a smell or a joke that no amount of staring would have preserved, and anyone who has found an old picture in a drawer knows the sudden warmth it can produce. Nobody is arguing that cameras damage memory in general. The question is narrower and, perhaps for that reason, more interesting: what do we give up when we replace attention with documentation?

There is also a quieter irony. We take photographs in order to remember, yet many of us rarely look at them again. The image is stored, tagged and forgotten, and the moment it was meant to preserve may have been experienced less fully than if the phone had stayed in the pocket. In this sense the photograph becomes a promise of future remembering that we are not always inclined to keep.

None of this calls for a ban on cameras, and the writer of this article has no intention of giving up his own. A more modest suggestion is available. Before raising the phone, we might pause for a few seconds and simply look, and then take the picture afterward, as a supplement to the experience rather than a substitute for it. The result may be a slightly slower walk through the museum, but a richer one.

title: The Tyranny of the Ranking
text:
Few numbers wield as much power over a school as its position in a published school ranking. A rise of three places is announced on banners and on websites; a fall of five is explained, with some embarrassment, in letters to parents. It is easy to see why. A ranking promises to reduce the complicated, many-sided life of a school to a single figure, and few of us can resist a figure that seems to tell us where we stand.

The difficulty begins when the figure becomes the goal. Consider a school, which I shall call Westbrook, that was determined to climb the ranking. Its principal noticed that the ranking depended heavily on the proportion of students achieving a certain grade in an examination. The fastest way to improve that proportion, it turned out, was not to teach better but to be more selective about who sat the exam. Students who were considered unlikely to succeed were quietly encouraged to take a different course. The school's ranking rose handsomely, and nobody had technically broken any rule.

The episode illustrates a principle that has been noticed in fields from economics to medicine: when a measure turns into a target, it ceases to be a good measure. The number was originally meant to reflect how well students were learning. Once schools began competing for the number itself, it came to reflect, in part, how skillfully they could manage it. What had been a useful instrument became a game, and like all games it rewarded cleverness rather than virtue.

It would be wrong, however, to conclude that rankings are worthless. Parents deserve some means of comparing schools, and without public figures there would be little to prevent a weak school from hiding behind vague reassurances. The sensible response is not to abolish the ranking but to be suspicious of what it can say. A single number cannot show whether a school is kind, whether it notices the shy child at the back of the class, or whether its graduates keep reading after the final exam.

Perhaps the wisest approach is to treat a ranking as a conversation starter rather than a verdict. When a school proudly announces its place, the intelligent question is not "How high?" but "How was that achieved, and at whose expense?" If the answer is a good one, the figure will survive the scrutiny. If it is not, the number was never telling the truth.

title: The Understudy
text:
Every evening in the theater, an audience settles into its seats and the lights go down, and somewhere in the building a person sits in a small room, fully dressed, waiting for something to go wrong. The understudy has learned a leading role line by line, movement by movement, without any guarantee that she will ever stand before a crowd. Tomas Reyes, an understudy at a regional theater, spent a whole season preparing for the part of a prince in a classic tragedy. He learned the lines, rehearsed the duels in an empty hallway, and attended the show every night, not knowing whether he would ever perform it.

Most of the time he did not. The leading actor was healthy, reliable and, as Reyes admits with a rueful smile, annoyingly punctual. Yet the preparation was never wasted, because it changed how he listened. Unlike the rest of the cast, he had to watch the whole performance as a possibility. A pause that seemed insignificant to others might, for him, be the only chance to find his breath on a night when it mattered.

Then one evening, forty minutes before curtain, the lead actor lost his voice. Reyes was handed a costume that did not quite fit and told, with admirable calm, that he was on. What followed was not, by his own account, a triumph. He forgot a line in the second act and recovered by repeating the previous one with unusual emphasis, a trick that, he suspects, only the other actors noticed. But the performance continued, the audience applauded, and nobody asked for their money back. In the theater, that counts as success.

The curious thing about the understudy's art is that its very best result is invisibility. If the substitute is competent, the evening passes much as it would have done, and the audience leaves without any sense that anything extraordinary has happened. A triumph is only discovered by those who know what was prevented. This makes the role an unusual one, demanding enormous preparation in exchange for the slimmest of recognition.

Reyes does not seem to resent this. He describes the experience as the best lesson in readiness he has ever received: a reminder that most of what matters in life happens not when we are prepared, but because we were. Some of us, he suggests, are always waiting in the small room, and the task is simply to be worthy of the call if it comes.

title: Old Bridges, New Questions
text:
For almost two centuries, the Haldane Bridge has carried the people of a small river town from one bank to the other. It is made of local stone, humped in the middle like a sleeping animal, and wide enough for a cart and a half. Last spring, engineers announced that it could no longer safely bear the weight of modern trucks. Within a week, the town was in uproar.

What is curious is the identity of the protesters. At the first public meeting, a succession of speakers rose to declare that the bridge was the soul of the town and that its loss would be unforgivable. Yet the local newspaper, with a mischievous sense of timing, reported that a great many of them had not crossed it on foot in years. They drove, as everyone does, over the newer road bridge a mile upstream, and regarded the old one as something to be admired from a distance, much as one admires a grandparent who lives in another city.

The council faced a decidedly contentious choice. Reinforcing the structure so that it could carry heavy traffic would cost more than a new bridge and would, by the engineers' own admission, change its appearance beyond recognition. Demolishing it and building a replacement on the same spot would be cheaper but would erase the very thing people claimed to cherish. After months of argument, a compromise emerged: a new road bridge would be built downstream, and the old one would be closed to vehicles and reserved for walkers and cyclists.

The solution satisfied almost nobody completely, which is perhaps the mark of a reasonable one. The heritage society complained that the old bridge would become a museum piece. Drivers grumbled about the additional detour. Yet something unexpected followed. Freed from traffic, the bridge began to be used in ways no one had anticipated: children fishing from its parapets, couples taking photographs in the evening, a weekly market on the Saturday after the harvest.

The episode suggests that the usual contest between preservation and progress is often misconceived. People rarely defend a monument because of its practical function; they defend it because of what it allows them to imagine about themselves. The bridge, in the end, may have been saved less by the arguments of the engineers than by the discovery that a place can be loved more intensely once it no longer has to be useful.

title: In Defense of the Difficult Book
text:
There is a fashionable assumption that reading should be effortless, and that a book which makes demands on its reader has somehow failed. Publishers promise "unputdownable" stories; reviewers praise novels that "fly by"; and any text that obliges us to slow down is likely to be accused of showing off. The assumption is understandable. We are busy, our attention is constantly under siege, and no one wishes to pay for confusion.

Yet there is a case to be made for the book that resists. Last year, a teacher named Ms. Adeyemi assigned her class a dense nineteenth-century novel, a work full of long sentences and unfamiliar references. By her own account, the early weeks were grim. Students complained that the prose was impenetrable, and a few suggested, not entirely in jest, that the author had been paid by the word. Then, gradually, something shifted. A student who had grumbled loudest began to read passages aloud simply because she enjoyed the sound of them. Another remarked that she had never before noticed how much she skipped when a text was easy.

That remark deserves attention. Easy reading allows the eye to travel faster than the mind, and what is understood quickly is often forgotten quickly too. A difficult book obliges us to stay with uncertainty, to hold a half-understood sentence in the head while the next one arrives, and to tolerate the unpleasant feeling of not yet knowing. These are not merely literary skills. They are the habits needed to follow any complex argument, whether in science, in law or in an ordinary disagreement with a friend.

It would be a mistake, however, to turn difficulty into a virtue in its own right. A mountain is not better than a hill merely because it is harder to climb, and some books are obscure only because their authors never learned to be clear. The reader owes no loyalty to unnecessary confusion. The point is rather that the reward is not always proportional to the speed at which it arrives, and that effort is sometimes the price of a deeper kind of pleasure.

None of this is to look down on the easy book. A light novel on a long journey is one of life's modest consolations, and nobody should be made to feel guilty for enjoying it. But a reader who never attempts anything harder may eventually find that the territory of the possible has grown smaller than it needs to be, and that the climb was less frightening than the fear of it.

title: The Night Sky We Have Misplaced
text:
For most of human history, the night sky was the common property of everyone who stepped outdoors after dark. It guided travelers, marked the seasons for farmers and provided a vast, silent canvas on which cultures wrote their myths. Today, a child growing up in a large city may never see the band of stars known as the Milky Way. It has not gone anywhere. It has simply been drowned out by the glow of our own lamps.

Scientists call this phenomenon light pollution, a phrase that sounds technical but describes something quite simple: light that is wasted, shining upward or sideways where nobody needs it. The consequences extend well beyond astronomy. Many nocturnal animals rely on darkness to feed or to find their way. Young sea turtles, for instance, instinctively head toward the brightest horizon, which for millions of years meant the moon on the water, and which on some coasts now means a hotel parking lot. Migrating birds can be drawn off course by lit buildings, and even plants, it appears, are affected by the length of their nights.

Faced with such arguments, people often raise a fair objection: surely lighting makes streets safer? The honest answer is that the evidence is more mixed than most of us assume. Some studies suggest that brighter streets reduce certain crimes, others find little effect, and a harsh glare can actually make it harder to see what lies in the shadows. What seems to matter is not the amount of light but the way it is used. A lamp that points downward lights the sidewalk just as effectively as one that sprays light in every direction, while sending far less into the sky.

This distinction gives reason for optimism, because it means the problem is not a choice between safety and stars. Shielded fixtures, warmer colors and lights that dim when nobody is about are all available, and several towns that have adopted them report lower electricity bills as well as darker skies. The remaining obstacle is not technological but psychological. Darkness has long been associated with danger, and we tend to equate more light with more security, even when the facts are less obliging.

It would be extravagant to claim that the stars will save anyone's life. But there is something worth preserving in the experience of looking up and feeling small, and that experience is increasingly difficult to obtain. It is a curious kind of poverty to have built a civilization capable of reaching the moon and then to have mislaid the means of seeing the stars properly.

title: A Museum of Magnificent Mistakes
text:
It takes a certain nerve to open a museum devoted entirely to failure, and the Museum of Magnificent Mistakes has nerve in abundance. Housed in a former umbrella factory, a coincidence the staff insist is accidental, it displays more than two hundred inventions that, in one way or another, did not work. There is a boot that was meant to warm the wearer's feet and which, according to the label, achieved this chiefly by catching fire. There is a clock that apologized every morning for waking its owner. There is a bicycle so ingeniously designed that nobody ever managed to ride it.

The museum's chief attraction is, undeniably, its sense of humor. Visitors move through the galleries in a state of cheerful disbelief, and I confess that I laughed aloud in front of a self-stirring teacup that, as far as anyone can tell, only stirred itself when nobody was drinking. The curators know when to leave a ridiculous object alone, and the display cases are admirably free of the solemn commentary that spoils so many exhibitions.

Yet it is precisely here that my reservations begin. Behind every failed invention there is a story, and the story is usually more interesting than the joke. These were not fools. Most of the inventors were skilled people trying to solve a genuine problem, and several of the devices failed only because of poor timing, unlucky competition or a manufacturer who lost his nerve. The labels, however, rarely say why anything failed, and visitors leave knowing that a thing did not work without learning what that failure might teach. A museum of mistakes that never examines its mistakes is a little like a school that hands out grades and never explains the answers.

The gift shop, to be fair, is a triumph. It sells the clock that apologizes, in a version that has been improved to the point of working, and I spent considerably more there than I intended. I suspect that this is the gentlest irony of the whole enterprise: the only invention in the building that truly succeeds is the one that persuades us to buy a souvenir of the others.

I would recommend the museum without hesitation to anyone who enjoys an afternoon of laughter, and I would recommend it with some regret to anyone hoping to learn from the wreckage. With a few more sentences on each wall, it could have been something rare: an institution that makes us smile at the past and, at the same moment, think harder about the future.
